title: Bubble Tea Shop Supply Chain
subtitle: An in-depth exploration of the challenges faced by a beverage shop and strategies for addressing them.
html:
View full presentation · Prezi ↗

How a milk shortage becomes an operating risk

This project examines fresh-milk supply at Mrs.Angel, connecting sourcing, replenishment lead times, shelf life, product availability, and sales exposure. The central question is how a shop can keep serving drinks when its primary supplier is late while managing the cost of substitute purchases and inventory.

The presentation reports that milk-based drinks account for approximately 40% of total sales. A shortage therefore affects more than purchasing: it can remove popular products from the menu, disrupt the customer experience, and expose other prepared ingredients to waste.

The constraint between lead time and shelf life

The project maps the relationship between the primary supplier, delivery delays, insufficient daily supply, and store inventory. It uses a procurement cycle of at least three days and a fresh-milk shelf-life window of three to four days to explain why simply carrying more inventory provides limited protection.

Ordering too little can leave demand unmet; ordering too much increases spoilage risk. Emergency purchases at higher prices can also erode margins. Replenishment decisions therefore need to consider reliability, freshness, cost, and the volume that can actually be sold together.

Three layers of backup: sources, ingredients, and coordination

The responses described in the presentation include diversifying purchases through nearby retailers such as Life, Ozeki, and Seiyu. These sources provide short-term alternatives when the primary supplier cannot deliver on time.

A second layer uses ultra-high-temperature-treated (UHT) milk as a backup ingredient. A third strengthens supplier communication, delivery confirmation, and coordination of priority deliveries. Together, these measures address where ingredients can be obtained, what can substitute during a shortage, and how delivery status can be understood earlier.

Extending the response to customers

The presentation also recommends reward cards, automatic discounts, and customer surveys to connect operating responses with retention and feedback. These are proposed next steps intended to bring the customer experience into the management of supply changes.

Why the project matters

For a small beverage shop, supply-chain disruption becomes visible directly on the menu and in the customer experience. This analysis translates a shortage into operating decisions, extending procurement beyond purchase price to product continuity and the tradeoff between stockouts and waste.

The key is to design alternative sources, substitute ingredients, and delivery coordination together. Extra stock alone, or one additional supplier alone, does not fully address the risks associated with a short-life ingredient.

Adapted from the original presentation. Sales share, procurement timing, and shelf-life windows are case inputs, not universal product or supplier specifications. No quantified cost or revenue improvement is claimed.
